sense: send on a letter or message

terms.grammar: exemplum, exemplī n., with mittō, mittere, mīsī, missum; whose letter, the genitive
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.23.3: Caesaris litterārum exemplum tibi mīsī
Cic. Att. 1.17.1: epistulārum illīus exempla mīsistī
terms.comment: How Cicero and Atticus passed each other’s letters on: a copy (exemplum) sent to a third person, which is what forwarding an email does.

terms.gloss: carry through, deliver (a letter to its addressee)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 2.6.1: hās quam prīmum ad tē perferrī litterās
Sen. Ep. 3.1: epistulās ad mē perferendās (M-O)
M-O s.v. forward (mail, a letter or message)

terms.comment: Classically “bring, deliver, hand over” (Lewis & Short); Traupman’s word for forwarding.

phrases.english: I’ve forwarded you a copy of Caesar’s letter

phrases.latin: magna mihi varietās voluntātis et dissimilitūdō opīniōnis ac jūdicī Quīntī frātris meī dēmōnstrāta est ex litterīs tuīs in quibus ad mē epistulārum illīus exempla mīsistī
phrases.english: your letter, in which you forwarded me copies of his, has shown me how changeable my brother Quintus’s feelings are, and how different his views and judgement

sources: Lewis & Short: exemplum · Lewis & Short: mitto · Lewis & Short: perfero · Lewis & Short: defero
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. forward (mail, a letter or message). John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 318, 343.
